pages.text: Three Shakespeare Stories

image.note: Cover: a theatre stage, masks, twins, a love-potion

pages.text: Contents. Twelfth Night / Much Ado About Nothing / The Comedy of Errors.

Long ago in England, a writer named William Shakespeare made plays so clever and so funny that people still tell them today. Here are three of his merriest, full of twins, disguises, and glorious muddles. He loved nothing better than a mix-up put right.

image.note: An Elizabethan stage, players in costume

pages.text: A great storm wrecked a ship on a strange shore, and from the waves crawled a young woman named Viola. She had lost everything, even her twin brother Sebastian, who she feared was drowned. Alone in a strange land, she had to think fast.

image.note: Viola on a stormy shore

pages.text: Viola had a bold idea. She would dress as a young man, call herself Cesario, and seek work at the court of Duke Orsino. In those days a woman alone was in danger, but a lively young man could go anywhere. So Viola cut her hair, put on a doublet, and became Cesario.

image.note: Viola disguising herself as Cesario

pages.text: The Duke liked clever Cesario at once, and soon trusted him with a secret task. Orsino was in love with a lady named Olivia, but she would not even see him. "Go to her, Cesario," said the Duke. "Speak for me. Make her love me." And off went Cesario, with a heavy heart.

image.note: Orsino sending Cesario to Olivia

pages.text: Heavy, because here was the muddle: Viola, as Cesario, had fallen quite in love with the Duke herself. But she could not say so, for he believed she was a man. "I must woo Olivia for the very man I love," she sighed. "Was ever a girl in such a tangle?"

image.note: Cesario sighing, torn between duty and love

pages.text: It grew worse. When Cesario spoke to Olivia, so bright and bold, Olivia did not fall for the Duke at all. She fell for Cesario. "Away with the Duke," said Olivia, gazing at the messenger. "It is you I want." Now the tangle had three knots at once.

image.note: Olivia gazing, smitten, at Cesario

pages.text: There was foolery in that house too. Olivia's stern steward, Malvolio, was so puffed up and pompous that the servants played a trick, leaving a letter to fool him into grinning and wearing bright yellow stockings, sure it would win Olivia's love. He pranced so absurdly that she thought he had lost his wits.

image.note: Malvolio prancing in yellow stockings, grinning

pages.text: Then, into the middle of all this, walked a young man who looked exactly like Cesario. It was Sebastian, Viola's twin, not drowned after all, but saved and washed ashore nearby. Now two identical faces moved through the same town, and no one knew there were two.

image.note: Sebastian arriving, the twin of Cesario

pages.text: The muddle untangled in a rush. Olivia, meeting Sebastian and thinking him Cesario, asked him to marry her, and he, dazzled, said yes. Then Viola and Sebastian came face to face at last, twin before twin, and wept for joy to find each other alive.

image.note: Viola and Sebastian reunited, astonished

pages.text: So all was set right. Viola took off her disguise, and the Duke, who had grown so fond of Cesario, was delighted to find his friend was a woman he could marry. Olivia had her Sebastian, Viola had her Orsino, and the whole tangled knot came loose in laughter and two weddings.

image.note: Two happy couples, Viola in her own dress

pages.text: In sunny Messina lived a lady named Beatrice, with the sharpest tongue in all the land, and a soldier named Benedick, with the second sharpest. Whenever they met, they quarrelled gloriously, trading clever insults like swordsmen, each swearing they would never, ever marry.

image.note: Beatrice and Benedick trading witty barbs

pages.text: "I would rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me," said Beatrice. "And I," said Benedick, "will live a bachelor till I die." Their friends listened, and smiled, and hatched a merry plan. For everyone could see what the two of them could not.

image.note: Friends watching, plotting mischief

pages.text: So the friends set a gentle trap. They let Benedick overhear them saying, sadly, how deeply Beatrice loved him but was too proud to show it. And they let Beatrice overhear the very same about Benedick. Each was astonished. Each began, secretly, to soften.

image.note: Benedick hiding behind a hedge, overhearing

pages.text: It worked like magic. Believing himself loved, Benedick suddenly found Beatrice wonderful. Believing herself loved, Beatrice found Benedick not so bad after all. The two fierce enemies of marriage began, quietly, to fall in love, each sure it was all their own idea.

image.note: Benedick suddenly smitten, smartening himself up

pages.text: But a shadow crossed the happy house. A spiteful man told a wicked lie about Hero, a sweet young woman about to marry Benedick's friend Claudio. He made it seem she had been false, and Claudio, deceived, shamed her before everyone at the wedding, and poor Hero fainted away.

image.note: Hero fainting, the wedding in uproar

pages.text: It looked like disaster. But the truth has a way of climbing out. A bumbling night-watchman, quite by accident, overheard the villains boasting of their lie, and hauled them off to answer for it. The wicked plot unravelled, and Hero's goodness was proved to all.

image.note: Comical watchmen catching the schemers

pages.text: So the lie was undone, Claudio begged Hero's forgiveness, and their wedding went ahead after all, joyful this time. And Beatrice and Benedick, still pretending to bicker, agreed to marry too, silencing each other at last with a kiss. Much ado about nothing, and everything set right.

image.note: Two couples wed, Beatrice and Benedick mock-scowling

pages.text: Here is the maddest muddle of all. Long ago, twin baby boys were born to one family, and, on the very same day, twin baby servants joined the household, alike as two peas. Two of them even shared a name each: the masters both called Antipholus, the servants both called Dromio.

image.note: Two pairs of identical babies

pages.text: A shipwreck split the family in two. One Antipholus and one Dromio grew up in a distant city; the other pair grew up far away, never knowing their twins were alive at all. And then, one fateful day, the travelling pair sailed into the very town where their long-lost doubles lived.

image.note: A ship arriving at a busy port town

pages.text: Now imagine the chaos. Two men with the same face and name, each with a servant of the same face and name, all loose in one town on one day, and not one of the four knowing the others existed. Every person they met kept mistaking one for the other.

image.note: Townsfolk pointing, baffled, at look-alikes

pages.text: A merchant demanded money from the wrong Antipholus, who had never borrowed a penny. A wife welcomed the wrong Antipholus home to dinner, and shut her real husband out in the street, baffled and furious. A Dromio was scolded by a master who had never sent him anywhere.

image.note: A wife dragging the wrong Antipholus to dinner

pages.text: "Am I bewitched?" cried one Antipholus, as strangers greeted him like an old friend. "This town is enchanted!" cried a Dromio, blamed for errands he had never run. The mix-ups piled higher and higher, and everyone thought everyone else had gone quite mad.

image.note: Antipholus clutching his head in the market

pages.text: At last, when the muddle could grow no worse, all four were brought to the same square at the same moment. The town gasped. Two Antipholuses, side by side. Two Dromios, face to face. Slowly, the impossible truth dawned: there were two of each, twins long lost.

image.note: All four twins meeting at last in the square

pages.text: And with that, everything came clear. The old family, scattered by the shipwreck so many years before, was whole again at last: parents, sons, and servants, laughing and weeping and hugging in the square. One long day of glorious confusion had brought them all home.

image.note: The reunited family embracing

pages.text: Three plays, three tangles, three happy endings. Notice how Shakespeare loved a disguise, a twin, and a muddle, and how, however knotted things became, kindness and truth always combed them straight in the end. That is why, four hundred years on, we are laughing still.

image.note: The three stories as a merry montage

pages.text: Shakespeare wrote nearly forty plays: comedies to make you laugh, and others to make you gasp and weep. You have met three of the merriest. One day, when you are ready, the rest are waiting for you on the stage.
